To wince means to make a small, involuntary movement of your face or body in reaction to something painful, unpleasant, or uncomfortable — a brief flinch that you didn't consciously decide to make.

When someone winces, their face tightens — usually the eyes squeeze slightly shut, the eyebrows pinch together, and the corners of the mouth pull back or downward. Sometimes the shoulders or neck tense up too. It's a quick, fleeting movement. It happens in a split second and then it's over.

Think of someone getting an injection. Right as the needle goes in, their face scrunches for a moment. That's a wince.

This is the most important thing to understand about wince. You don't choose to do it. Your body does it on its own, faster than your brain can think. You might even try not to wince — a brave patient at the doctor's might clench their jaw and try to stay still — but the wince happens anyway, or you catch yourself just barely suppressing it.

This is what separates wince from a deliberate reaction. You choose to grimace to show someone you're in pain. You don't choose to wince — it just escapes from you.

Wince is triggered by three broad categories:

1. Physical pain or the anticipation of it
Touching a bruise, stubbing a toe, hearing the dentist's drill, watching someone else get hurt — all of these can make you wince. Notably, you don't even have to be the one in pain. Watching someone else take a bad fall can make you wince for them, because your brain instinctively reacts to perceived pain.

He winced as the doctor pressed against the swollen ankle.
She winced just watching him walk on the broken glass barefoot.

2. A harsh sound or sudden sensory assault
A loud screech, nails on a chalkboard, a horrible musical note, a very bright flash of light — sharp and unpleasant sensory input can make you wince.

The microphone let out a sharp screech, and everyone in the room winced.

3. Emotional discomfort — embarrassment, awkwardness, or cringe
This is a very common use of wince in modern language. When something is deeply awkward, embarrassing, or cringe-worthy, you can wince at it. Maybe you're reading an old text you sent years ago, or watching someone make a social blunder, or hearing a very bad joke.

He winced reading his old diary entries.
She made such an obvious lie that I winced for her.

In this emotional sense, there may not be a visible physical movement at all — the wince happens internally, in your mind, as a feeling of "ooh, that's painful to witness." English speakers often say "I winced inwardly" to describe this invisible, felt reaction.
The size of a wince — it's always small

A wince is never a dramatic reaction. It's not a scream, not a jump, not a sob. It's the smallest possible outward sign that something hurt or disturbed you. This smallness is built into the word. If the reaction is bigger — a full recoil, a cry, a dramatic cringe — you'd use a different word. Wince describes that brief, contained, almost-suppressed moment.

This is why wince often appears when someone is trying to be tough or composed, but the pain or discomfort is strong enough to break through just a little:

The soldier winced but said nothing.
She kept her voice steady, though she winced at his words.

• Flinch — very close to wince, but flinch is more about a physical recoil or pulling away (flinching from a blow), while wince is more about the facial expression of pain or discomfort. The two overlap a lot, but wince has a stronger association with the face and with emotional/social pain.
  • Grimace — a grimace is a deliberate or sustained expression of pain or disgust, more visible and longer-lasting than a wince. A wince is a flash; a grimace can be held.
  • Cringe — in its original sense, cringe is a physical shrinking away from something frightening or humiliating. In modern usage it overlaps with wince for awkward/embarrassing situations, but cringe carries a stronger sense of shame or secondhand embarrassment, and often implies more of a lasting feeling rather than a brief flash.

Wince is almost always intransitive — meaning it doesn't take a direct object. You wince; you don't wince something.

You combine it with prepositions to explain the cause:

  • wince at something → She winced at the sound.
  • wince with something → He winced with pain.
  • wince in something → She winced in discomfort.

You can also use it with an -ing clause to show what triggered it:

He winced, hearing the bone crack.

To wince is to make a small, involuntary tightening of the face (or body) — a brief flinch you can't fully control — in response to something physically painful, sensorially jarring, or emotionally uncomfortable.
